t: Shape the website before we build
c: Choose the decisions that change the design and implementation. The agent will use your saved answers as the working brief.

q.p: What should the site feel like?
q.w: This drives typography, color, spacing, imagery, and motion.
o: Strong typography, generous whitespace, restrained color, and subtle motion.
It creates a durable visual system and keeps the content—not decoration—as the focus.
Saturated color, expressive type, larger shapes, and more visible animation.
Dense grids, mono accents, compact spacing, and almost no decorative motion.

q.w: The first-screen message determines the page hierarchy and primary call to action.
o: Lead with the visitor's result, then support it with proof and process.
Outcome-first messaging is clearest for new visitors who do not yet know you.
Lead with a visual project gallery and let examples establish credibility.
Lead with identity and background; useful when personality is the main differentiator.

q.p: What belongs in the first release?
q.w: A smaller launch is faster to polish; extra sections increase writing and testing work.
o: Core proposition, proof, and primary call to action.
Every usable first release needs a clear entry point.
Selected case studies with outcomes and your contribution.
Background, working style, and a portrait or personal visual.
Articles or notes; valuable only if content is ready to maintain.
A focused conversion path with email, form, or booking link.

q.w: This changes form handling, privacy requirements, and launch testing.
o: No backend and minimal privacy overhead.
It is the smallest reliable launch surface.
A structured inquiry flow that requires delivery, spam, and failure handling.
Fast scheduling through an external service and its availability rules.
